analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy requirements for new cars and light trucks, roughly 25-50% above each maker's 1988 levels.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 17 cosponsors and three days of subcommittee hearings, never advanced past the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required each automaker to raise the average fuel economy of its passenger cars to its 1988 level plus 25% by model years 1996-2000, and plus 50% by 2001 and after, with minimum floors of 27.5 and 35 miles per gallon; light trucks would face similar targets with 20 and 25 mpg floors [S2][S3]. It also would have doubled civil penalties for repeated violations, adjusted penalties for inflation, required annual EPA reports on how far real-world fuel economy falls short of lab tests, and ordered studies of future regulation [S2][S3]. A manufacturer could petition to change a standard, but not below a set multiple of its 1988 performance [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, which held hearings over three days in April 1991, and then went no further [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households buying new vehicles after 1996, who would save on gasoline over the life of the car; the country as a whole through lower oil consumption and, explicitly, reduced carbon dioxide emissions, which the bill instructs the Transportation Secretary to weigh in setting standards [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Each manufacturer's fleet average would have to reach its 1988 fuel economy plus 25% for model years 1996-2000 and plus 50% from 2001, with minimum floors of 27.5 mpg for cars and 20-25 mpg for light trucks [S3].

The bill directs the Secretary to weigh 'the need to reduce carbon dioxide emissions' equally with other factors in any rulemaking on the standards, and requires consideration of lifetime fuel savings to consumers against any price increase [S3].
Civil penalties for manufacturers that repeatedly miss the standard by half a mile per gallon or more would double, and all maximum penalties would be adjusted for inflation [S2][S3].

The EPA would have to report annually on the gap between tested and actual on-road fuel economy and on how fuel economy deteriorates over a vehicle's life, and every dealer would have to receive at least 100 consumer fuel economy booklets a year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would bear the engineering and manufacturing cost of meeting higher targets and face doubled penalties for repeat violations; consumers partly, through some pass-through of those costs in new-vehicle prices, offset by fuel savings over the vehicle's life [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Higher standards raise engineering costs for manufacturers, some of which typically shows up in new-vehicle prices; the bill requires the Secretary to weigh that impact on manufacturers and consumers against lifetime fuel savings [S3].

The targets are pegged to each manufacturer's own 1988 fleet, so a maker whose 1988 cars were relatively inefficient would face a lower absolute requirement than a more efficient competitor, weakening the overall average improvement [S3].

The Secretary could lower a standard through a petition-driven rulemaking to the 'maximum feasible' level, which gives manufacturers a regular channel to seek relief, though only down to a floor of 115-130% of their 1988 performance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fuel savings accrue directly to households over the life of each vehicle, and the bill tried to keep honest accounting by requiring annual reports comparing lab-tested and real-world mileage. The main honest objections are upfront vehicle cost and the manufacturer-specific baseline formula, which let laggard automakers meet a lower bar. On balance the design pushes savings to consumers and cuts oil use while giving industry a defined petition process.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee, which held hearings on three days in April 1991, but no committee vote or floor vote ever followed, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 23, 1991 by Rep. Dan Glickman with 17 cosponsors (15 Democrats, 2 Republicans) [S4][S5].
Referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then on February 11, 1991 to its Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
The subcommittee held hearings on April 16, 17, and 25, 1991 — the last entry in the bill's action history [S5].
No markup, committee report, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, especially those most reliant on less fuel-efficient light trucks, avoided the higher targets and doubled repeat-violation penalties; oil producers kept demand that stricter standards would have trimmed. Households kept paying for the gasoline the bill would have saved them.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only measurable support, the 17 cosponsors, was mostly Democratic (15 of 17) with 2 Republicans, and the decisive inaction happened in a committee controlled by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would force each maker to raise fleet fuel economy 25-50% above its own 1988 level, with doubled penalties for repeat violations, forcing changes to vehicle lineups and spending on efficiency technology. Blocking it preserved the status quo, including the light-truck segment that was least efficient.
Higher fleet mileage directly reduces gasoline demand, so the bill's failure preserved fuel sales that stricter standards would have cut. The industry's interest ran against consumers' fuel savings.
Dealers would have had to stock and hand out at least 100 consumer fuel economy booklets a year, a modest administrative cost, while more efficient fleets could appeal to cost-conscious buyers.
